stories.headline: Suspicious letters sent to Colorado congressional offices as federal authorities investigate nationwide mailings
stories.summary:
Federal authorities are investigating letters containing "suspicious substances" that were mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide. Recipients have been urged to treat the mailings as potentially hazardous. The FBI, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police are conducting the investigation.

In Colorado, Democratic U.S. Reps. Jason Crow of Aurora, Joe Neguse of Lafayette and Brittany Pettersen of Lakewood said their offices received letters on Monday. Sen. John Hickenlooper said postal investigators intercepted a suspicious letter addressed to his Denver office. Crow said his staff is safe and his district office remains open, and he thanked the Aurora Police Department and federal agencies for their response.

The FBI said the mailings were sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and related election offices. Some of the letters contained an unknown substance. A notice from the Senate Sergeant at Arms warned that some letters may still reach their destinations, even as law enforcement works to intercept them.

stories.headline: Court hears lawsuit that could remove Amendment 87 graduated income tax from Colorado ballot
stories.summary:
A lawsuit over Amendment 87, which proposes a graduated income tax, was heard in court Monday, two weeks before Election Day. Arapahoe County resident Michael Andre Hancock, who lawyers confirmed is not the former mayor, sued Secretary of State Jena Griswold and the measure's proponents. The defendants include Chris deGruy Kennedy of the Bell Policy Center and Kiyana Newell of New Era Colorado.

The suit alleges the signature gathering and certification process was flawed, with 9,849 signatures in question. It claims 69 paid gatherers were not on the list of registered and trained petition circulators, and it also challenges the Secretary of State's signature review. If enough signatures were thrown out, the measure would fall short of the threshold for the ballot.

DeGruy Kennedy said evidence showed at most 33 circulators could have their signatures disqualified, not enough to remove the measure. Amendment 87 would replace Colorado's 4.4% flat income tax with graduated brackets and remove the flat rate from TABOR. Revenue would go to a Colorado Futures Account for education, health care and early child care. The measure is opposed by the governor and many business leaders, and it could conflict with Proposition 136, which would cap taxes at 4.4%.

stories.headline: Denver mayor rejects key City Council 2027 budget requests
stories.summary:
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston has declined several of the City Council's largest 2027 budget requests. The council is pushing for about $26 million in changes to restore services, bolster staffing and revive programs hit by earlier cuts. Johnston has warned that the city has little room for new spending, with revenue projected to grow only 1.1%.

His revised budget, released Monday, agrees to about $4.2 million in funding for Denver Health, business assistance, community events and two city offices. It also adds 10 emergency communications workers, three 311 call takers, two park rangers and three inspectors. He rejected $5.5 million more for rental assistance, $2 million for another sheriff recruitment class and an $8.9 million reallocation of transportation funding to street safety.

To pay for the changes, the mayor is drawing on the contingency reserve, existing departmental budgets and other sources. The reserve would fall from 2.06% to 2.01% of General Fund expenditures, just above the charter-required 2% minimum. The proposed General Fund is $1.684 billion, with public safety accounting for nearly all of the growth.

stories.headline: Work begins on $806 million I-270 project to replace bridges and add express lanes
stories.summary:
Transportation officials broke ground Monday in Commerce City on an $806 million, seven-year overhaul of I-270. The project covers the six-mile stretch between I-25 and I-70. It will widen shoulders, improve ramps and add tolled express lanes in each direction.

The corridor carries more than 100,000 vehicles a day and is a key freight route. A central focus is replacing 12 aging bridges, eight of which on the west end have exceeded their design life. CDOT Executive Director Shoshana Lew said funding had been the biggest obstacle to the project.

The project will be paid for through the state's $5 billion transportation package passed in 2021, toll revenue from the express lanes and about $170 million in federal funds. Adams County Commissioner Julie Duran Mullica said competition for limited transportation dollars was the hardest part of getting the work started. The interstate has gone more than 60 years without an upgrade.

stories.headline: 18 arrested, 31 firearms seized in organized crime investigation across Denver area
stories.summary:
Eighteen people, including four juveniles, were arrested and 31 firearms were seized after a 13-month investigation into organized criminal activity across the Denver area, police said. The investigation targeted 20 members of a local criminal organization.

According to a news release, the group was responsible for more than 20 criminal episodes affecting 13 jurisdictions. Those include Aurora, Bennett, Commerce City, Denver, Frederick, Firestone, Greeley and Parker.

The investigation also spanned Adams, Arapahoe, Denver, Douglas and Weld counties. Fourteen adults and four minors were taken into custody.

stories.headline: Aurora police gave nonsensical Spanish warnings before dog bit man, lawsuit alleges
stories.summary:
An excessive-force lawsuit headed to trial Monday alleges an Aurora police dog bit an unarmed Mexican tourist during a 2023 SWAT operation. Salvador Alonso Guerrero-Salmeron, who does not speak English, stayed in his rented bedroom on South Yampa Court on March 3, 2023. Officers had arrived to serve an arrest warrant on a different man in the home who had no connection to him.

Officers used a loudspeaker to order everyone out in English and poorly pronounced Spanish. Their attempt to warn of the police dog, Loki, was nonsensical, saying words a translator rendered as "Fart police, fart the wood." Guerrero-Salmeron had texted the woman he rented from, saying he believed intruders were in the home.

City attorneys for the four officers named as defendants argue they acted reasonably. They say he did not comply for more than an hour and the home's layout posed uncertainty. Arapahoe County District Judge Don Toussaint ruled a jury should decide whether the officers' actions were reasonable. The Aurora Police Department declined to comment.

stories.headline: Private jet broker ONEflight faces 10 lawsuits seeking $6.2 million after abrupt pause
stories.summary:
Colorado private jet broker ONEflight faces 10 lawsuits from former customers seeking a combined $6.2 million. The suits follow the company's abrupt closure in September.

The plaintiffs allege fraud and Ponzi-like schemes. The complaints stem from payments customers say they made to the broker before operations stopped.

stories.headline: Real Capital Solutions, Dunton Commercial acquire Denver Tech Center tower for $23.75 million
stories.summary:
Real Capital Solutions and Dunton Commercial purchased a 12-story building in the Denver Tech Center for $23.75 million earlier this month. The tower is known as Terrace Tower.

The deal marks the first real estate acquisition made together by the two companies.

stories.headline: Denver City Council gives first approval to eminent domain for East Colfax sidewalks
stories.summary:
Denver City Council gave first approval Monday to let the city use eminent domain to gain access to 39 private properties for East Colfax sidewalk improvements. The power would apply only if property owners decline to agree.

The measure advanced on first approval and will require further council action.

stories.headline: Nuggets coach David Adelman sets top-six seed as regular-season goal
stories.summary:
Nuggets coach David Adelman said Monday his team's regular-season expectation is a top-six finish in the Western Conference. He noted a top-six team can still win the West, and said Denver finished third last year and fourth the year before. Denver has hosted a first-round series in four consecutive years.

The Nuggets are among six incumbent Western playoff teams expected to repeat as the top six, along with the Thunder, Spurs, Timberwolves, Rockets and Lakers. Falling outside the top six means the Play-In Tournament. Vegas projects Denver as a No. 3 seed, with Minnesota and Houston within one win. Denver opens the season Thursday at Oklahoma City.

The deadline for 2023 draftees to sign extensions passed Monday with no deal for guard Julian Strawther. He will become a restricted free agent next offseason. He sprained his left knee in a preseason game last week.

topStory.headline: Bend, Oregon, School Shooting by 16-Year-Old Raises Questions About Parental Criminal Liability
topStory.summary:
A 16-year-old carried out a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, last week, killing three children and a teacher before he was fatally shot by a student's parent. Another child and a teacher were injured, officials said. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said a pump-action shotgun was found near the suspect, who had about 44 remaining rounds of ammunition.

Investigators are examining how the teenager obtained the firearm and ammunition, which Krantz described as part of an "active criminal investigation." A senior law enforcement official briefed on the case told CNN the gun had been purchased by the teen's mother. The official said the parents were interviewed and cooperated, and that a search warrant was executed at the family's home on Thursday, with computers and other electronics taken. Additional search warrants have been obtained to gain access to further records.

Oregon law generally prohibits anyone under 18 from possessing a firearm, with exceptions for certain long guns transferred by a parent or used temporarily for hunting or target practice. Whether those exceptions apply, and what the parents knew about any risk, are expected to be central questions. CNN law enforcement analyst Andrew McCabe said the case could lead to criminal charges against the parents, as in other recent cases, and CNN analyst Juliette Kayyem said the inquiry would likely focus on how the teen accessed guns and what his parents knew.

Recent prosecutions elsewhere provide precedent. In Michigan, James and Jennifer Crumbley were convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 10 to 15 years in prison after their 14-year-old son Ethan carried out a school shooting. In Georgia, Colin Gray was convicted of murder and sentenced to 15 years after his 14-year-old son Colt carried out a school shooting. In Wisconsin, Jeffrey Rupnow, 44, has pleaded not guilty to three felony charges for allegedly allowing his 15-year-old daughter access to firearms, with trial set for March.

Prosecutors in such cases have said the goal is to push gun-owning parents to secure firearms and prevent future school shootings. No charges have been announced in Oregon, and the investigation is in its early stages. Authorities have not said when decisions on potential charges will be made.
